title: Valid Anagram — character frequency comparison (26-size array or HashMap).

s1_definition.profdef: Two strings are anagrams if one is a rearrangement of the other, meaning they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies. The efficient check compares character frequencies: increment a count per character for the first string, decrement for the second, and the strings are anagrams if all counts end at zero and the lengths match. It runs in linear time, using a fixed-size array for a known alphabet or a HashMap for arbitrary characters.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares two account label strings to decide if one is just a shuffled version of the other, useful for detecting disguised duplicate labels. Imagine a set of counters, one per letter. You add one for each letter in the first label and take one away for each letter in the second. If every counter lands back at zero and both labels are the same length, they use exactly the same letters, so one is a rearrangement of the other.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count up for one string and down for the other, and equal lengths with all counts zero means anagram.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two strings are anagrams if one is a rearrangement of the other, meaning they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies. The efficient check compares character frequencies: increment a count per character for the first string, decrement for the second, and the strings are anagrams if all counts end at zero and the lengths match. It runs in linear time, using a fixed-size array for a known alphabet or a HashMap for arbitrary characters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares two account label strings to decide if one is just a shuffled version of the other, useful for detecting disguised duplicate labels. Imagine a set of counters, one per letter. You add one for each letter in the first label and take one away for each letter in the second. If every counter lands back at zero and both labels are the same length, they use exactly the same letters, so one is a rearrangement of the other.

**One line to remember:** Count up for one string and down for the other, and equal lengths with all counts zero means anagram.

sections.s2_technical:
One correct approach sorts both strings and compares them, which is n-log-n time. The faster approach counts character frequencies in linear time. The fastest check first compares lengths: if the two strings differ in length they cannot be anagrams, so you return false immediately, which also lets you safely use a single counting structure afterward.

For a known small alphabet such as lowercase ASCII, you use a fixed array of twenty-six integers. You walk the first string and increment the count at the index for each character, computed as the character minus the letter a. Then you walk the second string and decrement the corresponding count. Finally you check that every count is zero. If any count is non-zero, some character appeared a different number of times, so the strings are not anagrams. A neat optimization is to return false the moment a count goes negative during the second pass, since that means the second string has a character the first did not have enough of.

For an arbitrary character set, including Unicode or mixed content, you use a HashMap from character to count instead of the fixed array. You increment for the first string and decrement for the second, removing entries that reach zero, and at the end the map should be empty. The logic is identical; only the storage differs to handle an open alphabet.

A senior point is case and whitespace handling, which the problem definition must pin down. If the comparison should be case-insensitive or ignore spaces, you normalize both strings first, for instance lowercasing and stripping non-letters, because otherwise `A` and `a` would count as different characters. In banking label comparison I define the normalization explicitly so the behavior is predictable.

Another senior point is the length-first check as both a correctness and a performance guard. Comparing lengths up front rejects obvious non-anagrams in constant time and guarantees that a single balanced count array can detect any frequency mismatch, because if the totals are equal and no count is negative, no count can be positive either. Stating this invariant shows you understand why the single-array trick is sufficient.

A small finance-domain example: `if(a.length()!=b.length()) return false; int[] cnt=new int[26]; for(char c:a.toCharArray()) cnt[c-'a']++; for(char c:b.toCharArray()) if(--cnt[c-'a']<0) return false; return true;` validates an anagram in one balanced pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India screens pairs of account label strings to detect whether one is merely a shuffled rearrangement of another, which can indicate a disguised duplicate label created to evade a uniqueness rule. The screening runs on many pairs so it must be linear. Checking a valid anagram by frequency comparison is exactly this.

This is exactly how Valid Anagram works in Java — counting up for one string and down for the other and confirming all counts return to zero.

Problem 2 — Labels can differ only in letter case or contain spaces, so the comparison normalizes to lowercase letters first, and strings of different lengths are rejected instantly. This shows the normalization choice and the length-first guard.

What the code will do: an `AnagramChecker` with `isAnagram(String a, String b)` using a twenty-six-element count array with the length-first guard and the early-negative exit. The demo screens several label pairs.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the label pair `Listen` and `Silent`.

Step 1: we normalize both to lowercase letters, giving `listen` and `silent`, each six letters. The lengths match, so we do not reject early and proceed to counting.

Step 2: we walk the first label `listen` and increment counts: l becomes one, i becomes one, s becomes one, t becomes one, e becomes one, n becomes one. So six distinct letters each have count one.

Step 3: we walk the second label `silent` and decrement: s goes to zero, i goes to zero, l goes to zero, e goes to zero, n goes to zero, t goes to zero. At no point does a count go negative, because every letter in `silent` exists with enough supply in the counts from `listen`.

Step 4: after the second pass every count is zero, so the method returns true, confirming `Listen` and `Silent` use exactly the same letters and are anagrams.

Step 5: for `Rajesh` and `Priya`, the normalized lengths are six and five, which differ, so the length-first guard returns false immediately without any counting. For `Debit` and `Bited`, both normalize to the same five letters and all counts balance to zero, so the result is true.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z INFO 'Listen' vs 'Silent' → IS anagram
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z INFO 'Rajesh' vs 'Priya' → different length, not anagram
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z INFO Result = false
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z INFO 'Debit' vs 'Bited' → IS anagram
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z INFO Result = true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "Listen", "Silent"
    │ normalize → "listen", "silent"
    ▼
  length equal? yes → count up for first, down for second
    │ +l+i+s+t+e+n   then  -s-i-l-e-n-t
    │ any count < 0? no
    ▼
  all counts == 0 → true
    ▼
  Output: anagram yes/no  (length mismatch → false early)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Anagram checks whether one string is a rearrangement of another, meaning they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, and I solve it in linear time with a balanced frequency count. I first compare lengths, because strings of different length can never be anagrams, and that constant-time guard both rejects obvious cases and makes a single count structure sufficient. Then I increment a count per character for the first string and decrement for the second.

The key invariant is that if the lengths are equal and no count ever goes negative while decrementing, then all counts must end at zero, so the strings are anagrams. That is why I can return false the instant a count goes negative during the second pass, since that means the second string has more of some character than the first supplied. For a known small alphabet like lowercase ASCII I use a fixed array of twenty-six counts for constant space; for an open or Unicode alphabet I use a HashMap with the same up-and-down logic.

I always pin down normalization, because the problem's intent decides it. If the comparison should ignore case or spaces, I lowercase and strip non-letters first, otherwise an uppercase and lowercase version of the same letter would be treated as different characters. Being explicit about normalization keeps the behavior predictable, which matters when the result drives a business rule.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to screen pairs of account labels for shuffled duplicates, a label that is just a rearrangement of an existing one created to evade a uniqueness rule, running linearly over many pairs. Explaining the length-first guard, the balanced count invariant, the early-negative exit, and the explicit normalization shows the interviewer that I understand why the single-array trick is correct, not merely that it works.
